claim: Asia is considered an important source of influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics, owing to large, diverse viral reservoirs in poultry and swine.
source: Asia is considered an important source of influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics, owing to large, diverse viral reservoirs in poultry and swine.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about influenza virus reservoirs in Asia.

claim: There is strong evidence that the first human outbreak of pdmH1N1 occurred in Mexico in early 2009.
source: There is strong evidence that the first human outbreak of pdmH1N1 occurred in Mexico in early 2009.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on the pandemic outbreak location.

claim: No related swine viruses to pdmH1N1 have been detected in Mexico or any part of the Americas prior to this study.
source: However, no related swine viruses have been detected in Mexico or any part of the Americas
evidence: This is supported by the absence of detection in previous surveillance efforts.

claim: The most closely related ancestor viruses to pdmH1N1 were identified in Asian swine prior to this study.
source: to date the most closely related ancestor viruses were identified in Asian swine.
evidence: This is supported by previous phylogenetic analyses of swine influenza viruses.

claim: 58 new whole-genome sequences from IAVs collected in Mexican swine were generated for this study.
source: Here, we use 58 new whole-genome sequences from IAVs collected in Mexican swine
evidence: This is directly stated as the data generated for the study.

claim: The swine virus responsible for the 2009 pandemic evolved in central Mexico.
source: Here, we use 58 new whole-genome sequences from IAVs collected in Mexican swine to establish that the swine virus responsible for the 2009 pandemic evolved in central Mexico.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses of the new sequence data.

claim: The 2009 pandemic arose from a region not considered a pandemic risk.
source: This finding highlights how the 2009 pandemic arose from a region not considered a pandemic risk
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that the pandemic originated in Mexico rather than Asia.

claim: An expansion of IAV diversity in swine resulted from long-distance live swine trade.
source: owing to an expansion of IAV diversity in swine resulting from long-distance live swine trade.
evidence: This is supported by phylogeographic analysis and trade data showing viral introductions correlating with swine imports.

claim: pdmH1N1 was a novel reassortant virus comprised of segments from three major swIAV lineages.
source: At the onset of the 2009 influenza pandemic, whole-genome sequencing revealed that pdmH1N1 was a novel reassortant virus comprised of segments from three major swIAV lineages (Garten et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous genomic characterization of pdmH1N1.

claim: Segments PB2, PB1, PA, NP and NS of pdmH1N1 were derived from a triple reassortant H3N2 swine virus (TRsw) that originated in North American swine during the mid-1990s.
source: segments PB2, PB1, PA, NP and NS were derived from a triple reassortant H3N2 swine virus (TRsw) that originated in North American swine during the mid-1990s
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous genomic characterization of pdmH1N1.

claim: The HA (H1) segment of pdmH1N1 derived from the classical swine H1N1 lineage (Csw) that has circulated in North American swine since the 1918 pandemic.
source: the HA (H1) segment derived from the classical swine H1N1 lineage (Csw) that has circulated in North American swine since the 1918 pandemic
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous genomic characterization of pdmH1N1.

claim: The NA (N1) and MP segments of pdmH1N1 were related to the avian-like Eurasian swine lineage (EAsw) that emerged in European pigs in the late 1970s.
source: and the NA (N1) and MP segments were related to the avian-like Eurasian swine lineage (EAsw) that emerged in European pigs in the late 1970s.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous genomic characterization of pdmH1N1.

claim: Genetic and epidemiological evidence indicate that the first outbreak of pdmH1N1 occurred in humans in Mexico.
source: Genetic and epidemiological evidence indicate that the first outbreak of pdmH1N1 occurred in humans in Mexico (Brockmann and Helbing, 2013; Chowell et al., 2011; Lemey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic and epidemiological studies.

claim: EAsw viruses had never been detected in swine in any part of the Americas prior to this study, including Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, Peru, Canada, and the United States.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous surveillance studies in the Americas.

claim: Asia was the only region where TRsw, Csw, and EAsw viruses were known to co-circulate in swine at the time of the 2009 pandemic.
source: At the time, Asia was the only region where TRsw, Csw, and EAsw viruses were known to co-circulate in swine (Zhu et al., 2013).

claim: Asia is a global source of novel human seasonal influenza viruses.
source: Asia is a global source of novel human seasonal influenza viruses (Lemey et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2008)

claim: Avian viruses associated with the pandemics of 1957 and 1968 originated from Asia.
source: avian viruses associated with the pandemics of 1957 and 1968 (Kawaoka et al., 1989)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on pandemic origins.

claim: Asia is the only region where TRsw, Csw, and EAsw are known to exchange segments through reassortment.
source: Asia is the only region where TRsw, Csw, and EAsw are known to exchange segments through reassortment (Lam et al., 2011; Poonsuk et al., 2013; Takemae et al., 2008; Vijaykrishna et al., 2011).

source: In the years following the pandemic, new surveillance in Mexican swine has identified Csw, TRsw, and pdmH1N1 and seasonal H3N2 viruses of human origin (Nelson et al., 2015a)

claim: The majority of swIAVs in previous analyses were collected in northern and eastern Mexico.

source: Among the 58 swIAVs newly sequenced from Mexico, genome segments were identified from all three major swIAV lineages (Csw, TRsw, and EAsw) and all three major human IAV lineages of the 21st century (H3N2, pdmH1N1, and pre-pandemic H1N1)

source: Except for TRsw (genotype 5) and pdmH1N1 (genotype 6), no other IAV lineages were identified intact in Mexican swine

source: evidence of frequent reassortment between viral lineages.

claim: Of the 12 genotypes identified in Mexican swine, 10 were reassortants.
source: Of the 12 genotypes identified, 10 were reassortants.

source: Four genotypes were triple reassortants

source: genotype 1 contains all three swine lineages (Csw/TRsw/EAsw)

claim: Human-origin viruses were observed in all regions of Mexico.
source: Although human-origin viruses were observed in all regions of Mexico

source: A high degree of population structure was observed among swIAV populations in Mexico's northern, central, and eastern regions.

source: Viruses collected in Sonora, Yucatan, Puebla, and Jalisco/Guanajuato/Aguascalientes consistently were positioned in different sections of the phylogenetic trees inferred for individual genome segments (Figure 3)

source: Viral gene flow was not frequently observed between Mexico's northern, eastern, and central regions (Figures 3,4A)

source: a contrast to the frequency of inter-regional IAV migration observed in US swine herds, driven by ongoing long-distance movement of animals (Nelson et al., 2011).

source: The only evidence for a migration event between two Mexican regions that is observed for multiple segments involves a single Yucatan virus (AVX-57) that is closely related to Jalisco viruses, evidence of Jalisco-to-Yucatan migration (Figure 4A, Figure 3—source data 1).

source: Viral migration occurred frequently between states in Mexico's central-west region, as evidenced by the clustering of viruses from Jalisco, Guanajuato, and Aguascalientes within the same phylogenetic clades (Figure 3—source data 1).

source: Time-scaled phylogenies suggest that viral introductions from US and European swine into Mexico have occurred periodically for at least two decades

source: No Mexican swIAVs were closely related to pdmH1N1 on the NS tree.

source: Both Guanajuato and Jalisco viruses are related to pdmH1N1 on the NP tree.

source: Genotype 1 viruses emerged multiple times in central Mexico

source: The identification of EAsw NA and MP segments in central Mexican swine is notable, given that these segments were associated with enhanced respiratory droplet transmission in animal models (Lakdawala et al., 2011; Yen et al., 2011).

claim: The EAsw MP segment is associated with zoonotic transmission of swIAVs at agricultural fairs in the US.
source: The EAsw MP segment also is associated with zoonotic transmission of swIAVs at agricultural fairs in the US (Bowman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous epidemiological study.

claim: The detection of EAsw in Mexico suggests that even relatively low levels of livestock movement can disseminate a highly transmissible virus such as IAV long distances.
source: The detection of EAsw in Mexico suggests that even relatively low levels of livestock movement can disseminate a highly transmissible virus such as IAV long distances
evidence: This is inferred from the finding of EAsw in Mexico despite limited imports from Europe.

claim: Imported live swine are not routinely tested for influenza.
source: Presently, imported live swine are not routinely tested for influenza.
evidence: This is stated as current practice based on knowledge of import procedures.

claim: The emergence of the 2009 pandemic virus was closely linked to the increase in Mexico's imports of live swine during the 1990s and the influx of new influenza virus lineages from the United States and Europe.
source: The emergence of the 2009 pandemic virus was closely linked to the increase in Mexico's imports of live swine during the 1990s and the influx of new influenza virus lineages from the United States and Europe.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation between trade data and viral introductions.

claim: Asia-to-Mexico viral migration cannot be ruled out, owing to possible omissions in reported imports and exports of swine and gaps in sequencing of viruses in swine globally.
source: At this time we cannot rule out Asia-to-Mexico viral migration, owing to possible omissions in reported imports and exports of swine and gaps in sequencing of viruses in swine globally.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty due to data limitations.

claim: All that is known about the nature of international swine production and trade suggests that Asia-to-Mexico viral movement is unlikely.
source: However, all that is known about the nature of international swine production and trade suggests that this direction of viral movement is unlikely.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of global swine trade patterns.

claim: Long-distance trade of pigs from Europe, the United States, and Canada to countries in Asia and South America occurs primarily to import high-efficiency European and North American breeding lines.
source: Long-distance trade of pigs from Europe, the United States, and Canada to countries in Asia and South America occurs primarily to import high-efficiency European and North American breeding lines.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of global swine trade practices.

claim: There are no known economic incentives (and strong economic disincentives) for the illegal trade of pigs from Asia and Mexico.
source: there are no known economic incentives (and strong economic disincentives) for the illegal trade of pigs from Asia and Mexico.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of economic factors in swine trade.

claim: Globally, Asia is overwhelmingly a net importer of swine from Europe and North America, with extremely little export of Asian pigs or their viruses to any other continents.
source: Globally, Asia is overwhelmingly a net importer of swine from Europe and North America, with extremely little export of Asian pigs or their viruses to any other continents (Nelson et al., 2015c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous analysis of global swine trade.

claim: Mexico has reported export of live swine to several countries in Latin America (Belize, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, El Salvador).
source: Mexico has reported export of live swine to several countries in Latin America (Belize, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, El Salvador).
evidence: This is based on trade data.

claim: The total volume of Mexico's live swine exports during 1996–2012 amounts to only one-tenth of Costa Rica's over the same time period, and one-thirtieth of Brazil's.
source: However, the total volume of Mexico's live swine exports during 1996–2012 amounts to only one-tenth of Costa Rica's over the same time period, and one-thirtieth of Brazil's.
evidence: This is based on trade data analysis.

claim: Mexico is considered an ecological sink for swine influenza viruses, with limited opportunity for viral export to other countries.
source: Mexico is therefore considered an ecological sink for swine influenza viruses, with limited opportunity for viral export to other countries (Nelson et al., 2015c).
evidence: This is inferred from the trade data and supported by citation.

claim: The unexpected detection of EAsw in Mexico highlights the need to revisit outdated assumptions about the spatial distribution of IAVs in swine populations globally.
source: The unexpected detection of EAsw in Mexico highlights the need to revisit outdated assumptions about the spatial distribution of IAVs in swine populations globally
evidence: This is an inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Long-distance live swine movements have the capacity to disseminate viral diversity between continents.
source: given the capacity of long-distance live swine movements to disseminate viral diversity between continents.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of this study.

claim: Surveillance of swIAVs remains highly imbalanced on a global scale and low compared to avian surveillance.
source: it remains highly imbalanced on a global scale and low compared to avian surveillance (Nelson and Vincent, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous review of surveillance efforts.

claim: Recent detections of novel swIAVs in regions that traditionally have not conducted surveillance in swine, including Latin America and South-east Asia, underscore the importance of expanding surveillance in under-sampled regions with high densities of swine.
source: Recent detections of novel swIAVs in regions that traditionally have not conducted surveillance in swine, including Latin America and South-east Asia, underscore the importance of expanding surveillance in the large number of under-sampled regions with high densities of swine (Cappuccio et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2015a; Ngo et al., 2012; Perera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent surveillance studies.

claim: China remains an important source of zoonotic influenza viruses with pandemic potential.
source: China remains an important source of zoonotic influenza viruses with pandemic potential
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of influenza emergence in China.

claim: The identification of strong regional variations in swIAV diversity in Mexico highlights the importance of capturing swIAV diversity across China's heterogeneous regions.
source: and the identification of strong regional variations in swIAV diversity in Mexico highlights the importance of capturing swIAV diversity across China's heterogeneous regions.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for surveillance in China.

claim: Data on poultry movements within and between countries are lacking, limiting understanding of the role of trade in the spatial dynamics of IAVs in domestic birds.
source: Data on poultry movements within and between countries are similarly lacking, limiting our understanding of the role of trade in the spatial dynamics of IAVs in domestic birds.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of data availability.

claim: The ability to predict future pandemics will require intensified viral surveillance and an understanding of how economic forces and international trade policies affect changes in animal movements and production practices that drive viral emergence.
source: Our ability to predict future pandemics will require intensified viral surveillance and an understanding of how economic forces and international trade policies affect changes in animal movements and production practices that drive viral emergence.
evidence: This is an inference about future research needs based on the findings.

claim: Swine influenza isolates were obtained from samples submitted to Avimex laboratories (Mexico) for confirmation diagnostics of pigs with respiratory syndrome.
source: Swine influenza isolates were obtained from samples submitted to Avimex laboratories (Mexico) for confirmation diagnostics of pigs with respiratory syndrome.
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: The samples covered years 2010 (1 sample), 2011 (6 samples), 2012 (34 samples), 2013 (14 samples) and 2014 (3 samples).
source: The samples covered years 2010 (1 sample), 2011 (6 samples), 2012 (34 samples), 2013 (14 samples) and 2014 (3 samples).
evidence: This describes the temporal distribution of samples.

claim: All samples came from large commercial facilities from 6 states: Sonora (8 different farms), Jalisco (6 farms), Guanajuato (3 farms), Puebla (2 farms), Yucatan (2 farms) and Aguas Calientes (1 farm).
source: All samples came from large commercial facilities from 6 states: Sonora (8 different farms), Jalisco (6 farms), Guanajuato (3 farms), Puebla (2 farms), Yucatan (2 farms) and Aguas Calientes (1 farm).
evidence: This describes the geographic distribution of samples.

claim: Nine triple reassortant Mexican swIAVs were excluded from the phylogenetic analysis because they were outliers in root-to-tip divergence.
source: We excluded nine triple reassortant Mexican swIAVs (e.g., A/swine/Mexico/Mex19/2010(H1N1), Figure 3—figure supplement 1) that had shorter branch lengths than expected given their year of sampling, an indication of possible errors in sequencing or assembly.
evidence: This describes the quality control procedure for the phylogenetic analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
